rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states that the technical documentation must include 'a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run', citing Annex IV point 1(e), which conveys the substance of the requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The Regulation contains no "medium-risk" tier, and the operator's AI system is high-risk. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met: point (a), it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is listed in Annex I, Section A; and point (b), that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market. The operator's facts satisfy both, and the trigger is the existence of third-party assessment, not the device's sectoral risk class, so the MDR "medium-risk" label does not carry across, classification under Article 6(1) is binary. Consequently the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply and, under Article 43(3), are assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure, with Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of 4.6 also applying. The Annex VII point 4.2 application comprises the provider's name and address (4(a)), a written declaration that no same application is lodged elsewhere (4(b)), and the Annex IV technical documentation (4(c)).
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: Answer correctly states there is no 'medium-risk' category and identifies the AI system as high-risk
Answer states the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, specifically the MDR
Answer confirms the product undergoes third-party conformity assessment as required under condition (b)
Answer explains that both conditions are cumulative under Article 6(1) and that classification is independent of the device's sectoral risk class
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and it is not high-risk on that ground alone. Article 5(1) lists the prohibited practices exhaustively, and biometric verification confirming that a specific natural person is who he or she claims to be is not among them. Annex III, point 1(a) expressly excludes from the remote biometric identification use-case AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is that confirmation, so Article 6(2) is not triggered. It would still be high-risk if it falls under Annex I as a product safety component or under another Annex III use-case.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states that biometric verification for confirming identity is not among the prohibited practices in Article 5(1), which directly addresses the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the system is not high-risk on the basis of Annex III.1(a), satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The answer cites the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems with the sole purpose of confirming identity, conveying the substance of criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight measures are governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use (Article 14(1)).
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that human oversight measures are governed by Article 14.
The answer includes the substance that high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so they can be effectively overseen during use, which captures the requirement in Article 14(1).
The answer does not mention that the aim of human oversight is to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, even though this is required by Article 14(2).
The answer does not state that oversight measures may be built in by the provider or implemented by the deployer, as specified in Article 14(3).
The answer does not include any of the specific capabilities overseers must have, such as understanding, monitoring, interpreting, overriding, or halting the system, as detailed in Article 14(4).
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral language in the third person, clearly identifying the governing article and summarising a key requirement without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer affirms the existence of exceptions in Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly states that (c) and (d) still apply.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices laid down in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). This is the highest of the Regulation's three ceilings, sitting above the EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % tier for the operator and notified-body obligations listed in Article 99(4) and the EUR 7 500 000 / 1 % tier for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities (Article 99(5)). Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage and the fixed amount rather than the higher (Article 99(6)). The fine must in each case be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and set with regard to the gravity and nature of the infringement and the circumstances listed in Article 99(7), Member States laying down the penalty rules under Article 99(1).
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fine to non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices in Article 5, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is in neutral, professional language, directly quoting the definition from the Act in a clear and concise manner suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases), capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems carry transparency duties under Article 50, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer notes that minimal-risk systems avoid high-risk obligations and mentions voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95, thereby stating the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming the possibility.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market results in being considered a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering condition.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The objective of the AI Act is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation (Article 1(1)).
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of improving the functioning of the internal market.
The candidate answer states the substance of promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.

The candidate answer states the substance of ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights, including democracy, the rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI systems.
The candidate answer states the substance of supporting innovation.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as the initial verdict, which matches the required 'No' in criterion 1 and is unambiguous.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and cites the correct provision, Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly excludes profiling of natural persons from the derogation by stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which captures the exception in the criterion.
The answer references Article 6(4) and states the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, which matches the requirement in the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine under that Article, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. That review power is not confined to annulment on legality grounds: the Court may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, in either direction. The fines so reviewable are those the Commission may impose on providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 101(1), not exceeding 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where the provider intentionally or negligently committed one of the listed failures. The Commission must first communicate its preliminary findings and give the provider an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)), and any fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)).
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine', which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel, reduce or increase the fine', satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes 'may reduce the fine' as part of its explicit list of powers, satisfying criterion 3.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may...increase the fine', and further clarifies that the Court may substitute its own assessment 'in either direction', satisfying criterion 4.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Information for registration in the EU database (Article 49 requires providers (and deployers that are public authorities) to register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database (Article 71) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.): Section A populated by provider / authorised representative (system name, intended purpose, components/datasets, design specifications, instructions for use, CE marking, conformity-assessment certificate, supervisory authority); Section B for Article 6(3) non-high-risk assessments; Section C populated by public-authority deployers. Public-access carve-out for law enforcement / migration / asylum / border-control systems. EU database for high-risk AI systems and GPAI models registered under Articles 49 + 60, set up and managed by the Commission, with public + restricted-access sections; data is machine-readable + navigable + searchable. Requires providers (and deployers that are public authorities) to register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database (Article 71) before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.

AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.

Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), the provider must supply concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use, in a format accessible to deployers, containing at least six categories of information. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative (point (a)). Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including intended purpose; the level of accuracy with its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15 against which the system was tested and validated; known or foreseeable circumstances of intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse giving rise to Article 9(2) risks; technical means to explain output; performance regarding specific persons or groups; input-data specifications and information on the training, validation and testing datasets; and information enabling deployers to interpret and use the output appropriately (point (b)). Third, any pre-determined changes to the system and its performance fixed at the initial conformity assessment (point (c)). Fourth, the Article 14 human oversight measures, including technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs (point (d)). Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and necessary maintenance and care measures including their frequency and software updates (point (e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs under Article 12 (point (f)).
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity and contact details as required by Article 13(3)(a).

The answer explicitly references Article 14 human oversight measures and includes technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs, satisfying Article 13(3)(d).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, such as civil society organisations and academia, and may cover one or more AI systems taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems (Article 95(3)). The bodies required to encourage and facilitate their drawing up are the AI Office and the Member States, in respect of codes, including related governance mechanisms, fostering voluntary application, to AI systems other than high-risk ones, of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices (Article 95(1)). The AI Office and the Member States must likewise facilitate codes on voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, based on clear objectives and key performance indicators (Article 95(2)), and must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when doing so (Article 95(4)). Annex VII, point 4 governs the provider's technical-documentation application to a notified body and contains no rule on codes of conduct.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The answer states that codes may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or both, which captures the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly mentions involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, satisfying criterion 2.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner as written policies, procedures and instructions, and covering at least thirteen aspects. These are: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment procedures and management of modifications to the system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification; (c) the same for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, and their frequency; (e) technical specifications, including standards, and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full, the means used to meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management across acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of post-market monitoring under Article 72; (i) serious-incident reporting procedures under Article 73; (j) handling of communication with national competent and other authorities, notified bodies, operators, customers and interested parties; (k) record-keeping systems and procedures; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply measures; and (m) an accountability framework allocating management and staff responsibilities for all those aspects. Implementation must be proportionate to the provider's organisation size while preserving the required rigour and level of protection (Article 17(2)); providers already subject to sectoral Union QMS obligations may integrate these aspects into that system (Article 17(3)), and financial institutions subject to Union financial services internal-governance rules are deemed compliant except for points (g), (h) and (i) (Article 17(4)).
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the requirement for a regulatory compliance strategy including conformity assessment and modification management.
The answer includes design, development, quality control, and verification techniques and procedures under points (b) and (c).
The answer specifies examination, test, and validation procedures and their frequency under point (d).
The answer details data management procedures across the data lifecycle under point (f).
The answer explicitly references the Article 9 risk management system and the Article 72 post-market monitoring system under points (g) and (h).
The answer includes record-keeping systems and an accountability framework for management and staff under points (k) and (m).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose with clear enumeration and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) unless, and only in so far as, it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. First, Article 5(1)(h)(i): the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons. Second, Article 5(1)(h)(ii): the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack. Third, Article 5(1)(h)(iii): the localisation or identification of a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences listed in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of a maximum of at least four years. Use is confined to confirming a specifically targeted individual's identity and requires a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration under Article 49 (Article 5(2)).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, as well as a genuine threat of a terrorist attack, capturing the full substance of criterion 2.

The answer correctly identifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or execution of a penalty for Annex II offences punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence, satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise legal references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated; the technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, given content specificities and limitations, implementation costs and the generally acknowledged state of the art reflected in technical standards. This does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law for criminal-law purposes (Article 50(2)).
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: Answer states marking must be in machine-readable format.
Answer states marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
Answer includes that the solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
Answer references content specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art as factors for feasibility.
Answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input/semantics, and law-enforcement authorisation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, grammatically complete sentences and logical structure.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). That exclusivity displaces national market surveillance authorities for Chapter V itself; those authorities may only request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks, without prejudice to Article 75(3) (Article 88(2)).
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, citing Article 88(1) and reproducing its substance.
The candidate answer clearly states that the Commission entrusts implementation of these tasks to the AI Office, which matches the substance of the second criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a coherent and actionable manner.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing high-risk AI systems in real world conditions may be transferred to third countries only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). That condition is not free-standing: it is one of the cumulative conditions of Article 60(4), all of which must be met, so a transfer is permissible only while the testing itself remains lawful, an approved real-world testing plan, registration of the testing, establishment in the Union or an appointed Union legal representative, and informed consent of the test subjects. The safeguards in question are those of Union data protection law, including its rules on international transfers and on special categories of data, and they operate alongside each subject's right to withdraw consent and obtain immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data (Article 60(5)). Article 60 imposes no further third-country-specific condition.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by explicitly requiring that 'appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented' for data transfers, which directly matches the requirement in Article 60.4.e.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a coherent and actionable manner for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions: (a) it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; or (b) based on a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Either route alone suffices. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption rather than a third condition: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under point (a) where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. Under Article 51(3) the Commission may amend those thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act to reflect the state of the art. The Annex III high-risk areas listed in the evidence have no bearing on this classification.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, as specified in Article 51(2).

The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, ex officio or following a qualified alert, based on equivalence to high-impact capabilities using Annex XIII criteria, is a valid route for classification.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives and not cumulative, and that either alone suffices, matching the unambiguous verdict required.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logically ordered way suitable for regulatory use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Classification under the Annex I route requires both conditions in Article 6(1) to be met cumulatively. Condition (a) is satisfied: the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed in Annex I, point 11. Condition (b) is not: a Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so it is not required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. The system could still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it falls within a listed Annex III use case.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions in Article 6(1) must be met cumulatively.
The answer correctly explains that the specified MDR Class I device is self-certified without notified body involvement, meaning no third-party conformity assessment is required.
The answer concludes that condition (b) fails and therefore Article 6(1) does not apply, directly stating the logical consequence.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically ordered and actionable.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift qualifies as high-risk, provided both cumulative conditions in Article 6(1) are met, and this applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift (or the AI system itself as a product) must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable here, as it applies only to systems classified through Annex III. Conformity assessment then follows Article 43(3): the procedure required under Directive 2014/33/EU, with the Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, making the affirmative position unambiguous.
The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifically references lifts under Directive 2014/33/EU as an example.
The answer clearly states that the product (the lift or the AI system itself) must be subject to third-party conformity assessment under the relevant Directive.
The answer explicitly describes the two conditions as 'cumulative' and states that 'both' must be met.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured, coherent prose with logical flow suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, professional, and uses the precise regulatory language without any self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: The two duties are cumulative, not alternative, and neither is displaced by the market surveillance authority's own evaluation. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it, as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the Article 44 certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. Article 79(1) supplies only the definition of risk (a "product presenting a risk" under Article 3, point 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, extended to fundamental rights); it imposes no duty and does not defer the provider's investigation to the authority. The authority's separate evaluation under Article 79(2) runs in parallel, and the provider must cooperate with it.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the duties are cumulative, meaning both actions are required.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's obligation to take immediate corrective action when non-compliance is suspected.
The answer explicitly states that under Article 20(2), the provider must immediately investigate the causes.

The answer clarifies that the investigation is the provider's duty and must be done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and notes that the provider's duty is not deferred to the market surveillance authority.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose suitable for regulatory advice; no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise compliance with the Section 2 requirements, the "where applicable" wording accommodates systems embedded in physical products or supplied on hardware, so the duty simply does not bite where no such conditions exist.
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms the model did not hallucinate, aligning with the required 'No, not hallucinated' verdict.
The answer cites Article 24(3) and accurately describes its requirement, confirming its applicability.
The answer explains that the duty applies only 'where applicable', clarifying that it pertains to cases involving physical media or embedded hardware, thus capturing the conditional scope.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained explanation without meta-commentary or informal address; logically structured and actionable.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: No, the AI Act does not regulate drones as such; classification turns on the AI system's intended purpose. Using AI on a drone to identify people around town engages Article 5(1)(h), which prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement save for its listed derogations, and otherwise falls under Annex III, point 1 (biometrics) as high-risk. A toy drone falls under Directive 2009/48/EC in Annex I, so per Article 6(1) it is high-risk only where the product must undergo third-party conformity assessment; used for non-toy applications, the Annex I route drops away and only the Annex III use-case route applies.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended use under Article 6, not the drone itself.
Correctly identifies use of AI in drone for identifying people in public as remote biometric identification, falling under Annex III(1)(a) as high-risk.
Explains that toy status does not determine classification, which hinges on intended use.
Clarifies that when a toy drone is used for other applications, only Annex III or Article 6(1) criteria apply based on use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information clearly for regulatory application.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed on that basis, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. The high-risk classification attaches to the system as placed on the market, whether by the Annex I product route (Article 6(1)) or because it falls within an Annex III use-case (Article 6(2)); the operator's legal team's conclusion that the new use is itself neither an Annex I nor an Annex III case does not de-classify the system you have already deployed. As deployer the operator must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure you use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), so a use outside the intended purpose is a breach unless the provider's instructions cover it. If you go further and substantially modify the system or change its intended purpose, Article 25 makes you a provider and you assume the full Chapter III provider obligations. Such off-label use is also reasonably foreseeable misuse to be estimated and evaluated in the risk-management system (Article 9(2)(b)). On logging: Article 26(6) requires the operator to keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk system, to the extent under the operator's control, for at least six months unless Union or national law provides otherwise; the provider's mirror duty is Article 19(1).
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the deployer cannot proceed with the new use, aligning with the required 'No' verdict.

The answer explains that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use and that deviating from intended use is not permitted, even if the new use alone would not trigger Annex III.
The answer affirms that the logging obligation under Article 26(6) applies to the high-risk system regardless of the specific use, as long as logs are under the deployer's control.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents actionable regulatory analysis.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. Clinical decision-support software guiding treatment choices is potentially high-risk under Article 6(1): as a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (or 2017/746), listed in Annex I, it is high-risk where it is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by that legislation and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service. Annex III is generally not the operative route here.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes', clearly affirming that the AI software is potentially high-risk.
The answer cites Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and explains the high-risk classification under 6(1), so it does not state the substance that Article 6(2) is the applicable provision.
The answer explicitly states that Annex III is 'not the operative route here', which contradicts the criterion requiring it to be satisfied based on Annex III (healthcare access/provision).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly explaining the regulatory basis.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four, no to the last. Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII.1, the information for downstream providers must include the date of release and methods of distribution (point (c)), the architecture and number of parameters (point (f)), how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable (point (d)), and the licence for the model (point (h)); Annex XII.2(c) requires only the type, provenance and curation methodologies of training data, not samples of outlier data.
criteria_text: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the date of release must be disclosed, in line with Annex XII.1(c).
The answer clearly includes architecture and number of parameters as required under Annex XII.1(f).
The answer addresses interaction with hardware or software under Annex XII.1(d), confirming disclosure is required where applicable.
The answer explicitly confirms license disclosure is required under Annex XII.1(h).
The answer correctly states that samples of outlier training data are not required, referencing Annex XII.2(c) which limits requirements to type, provenance and curation methodologies.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured with clear reference to legal provisions; no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not one of the Annex III areas; it is covered only indirectly. Annex III lists eight areas of high-risk use cases: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, points 1 to 8). Only a lettered use-case under one of those headings makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2). Health-related uses appear as specific use-cases within area 5: systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (Annex III, point 5(a)); risk assessment and pricing for natural persons in life and health insurance (Annex III, point 5(c)); and emergency-call triage and dispatch, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems (Annex III, point 5(d)). Clinical decision-support software instead normally becomes high-risk by the Annex I route: it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device requiring third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1); Annex I, point 12).
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The answer lists all eight areas from Annex III, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The answer unambiguously states 'No' and explains that healthcare decision making is not directly listed as an Annex III area, aligning with the correct interpretation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails cannot move an AI system out of the high-risk category: classification under Article 6 and Annex III turns on the system's intended purpose and whether it falls within a listed use-case, and Article 8(1) treats mitigation as the means of compliance, with the Article 9 risk-management system "taken into account when ensuring compliance," not as a route out of Chapter III. Only the Commission may add, modify or remove Annex III use-cases, by delegated act under Article 7(1), on the cumulative conditions that the system is used in a listed area and poses risk equivalent to or greater than existing entries, or under Article 7(3) for removal. Changing capabilities and intended use can change classification, but it cuts the other way procedurally: under Article 25(1)(b), (c), a substantial modification that leaves the system high-risk, or a change of intended purpose that makes a non-high-risk system high-risk, makes the modifier a provider bearing Article 16 obligations. Guardrails instead feed Article 13(3)(b)(i), (vii) instructions for use, intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable-misuse risks, explanatory capabilities, performance on specific persons or groups, input-data specifications, and output-interpretation information, and Article 12(2) logging traceability. Annex IV and Article 18 are not supported by the evidence here.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that guardrails do not alter high-risk classification and emphasizes the binary nature of risk categorization under Article 6, aligning with the substance of the criterion.
The answer does not state or imply any of the four Article 6(3) conditions for exemption; it discusses procedural and compliance aspects but omits the specific substantive conditions required.

The answer acknowledges that changing capabilities and intended use can affect classification, referencing Article 25(1)(b),(c), which supports the idea that redefining purpose may alter risk status if the new use falls outside high-risk criteria.
The answer fails to mention the profiling exception in Article 6(3), which mandates that systems performing profiling of natural persons are always high-risk, regardless of other changes.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, third-person regulatory tone; well-structured and coherent, with precise references to provisions without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted, and yes, the artificial nature must be disclosed; the lighter, law-enforcement-style relief does not apply. Nothing in the Regulation prohibits generating synthetic clinical images for teaching, and illustrative teaching material does not fall within any of the lettered use-cases under the education and vocational training heading of Annex III, so the university is not deploying a high-risk system under Article 6(2) and the Chapter III duties (Articles 26, 43, 49) are not triggered. The university is nonetheless a deployer of an AI system generating image content constituting a deep fake and must therefore disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph); the provider of the generating system separately owes the machine-readable marking and detectability duty (Article 50(2)). The only carve-out from that deployer duty is use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, which a university lecture does not meet. The attenuated "appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment" regime is confined to content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work; factual medical illustration is not such a work, so ordinary disclosure is owed.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. The tool is neither prohibited nor high-risk on these facts. Article 5(1)(d) is not engaged: it flags current-cart and checkout anomalies, objective, verifiable facts directly linked to possible theft supporting a human bag check, not a risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits. Article 5(1)(c) is not engaged either: there is no scoring over a period of time across unrelated social contexts.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No', which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer does not state the substance of criterion 2; it does not mention that Annex III.6 applies only when the AI is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities.

The answer does not state that a supermarket's tool is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, which is the substance of criterion 3; it focuses instead on Article 5 provisions without addressing the scope of Annex III.6 applicability.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register; clear, coherent structure without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2. Article 43(3) states expressly that the Section 2 requirements apply to high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Section A of Annex I (points 1 to 12, e.g. machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX, radio and pressure equipment, cableways, PPE, gas appliances, medical devices and IVDs; points 13 to 20 form Section B) and shall be part of that sectoral assessment. Crucially, where a Section A act lets the manufacturer opt out of third-party conformity assessment on the basis of having applied all harmonised standards, Article 43(3) permits use of that option only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all Section 2 requirements, so the operator's opt-out presupposes, rather than displaces, Section 2 compliance. Points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Classification is unchanged: Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are met. Article 43(1)(a) to (d) and the Annex VI internal-control route concern Annex III point 1 systems, not yours. Article 43(4) still requires a new assessment upon substantial modification. The evidence supplied contains no text for Article 41(1)(a)(i) to (iv).
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2', which matches the required 'No' verdict.

The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing Article 43(3) and explaining that these requirements 'shall be part of that sectoral assessment'.

The answer explains that the opt-out is permitted only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones, directly reflecting the condition in Article 43(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance professional.
